summary: Defines a Sieve extension that lets a mail filter push a notification when a message arrives, instead of making users poll for new mail. It leaves the notification method open, expecting things like XMPP or SMS to be used. This is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 8580.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5435 extends the Sieve email-filtering language so a script can request a notice when a message arrives. It also lets scripts check whether a notification method is supported before using it.

subtitle: Add rule-based notifications to Sieve mail filtering, with checks for supported delivery methods.

tldr.problem: Users often check repeatedly for new mail. This polling takes time and uses server resources.
tldr.mechanism: The enotify extension adds a notify action, tests for method support and availability, and a modifier for safely placing text in a URI.
tldr.outcome: Sieve scripts can request notifications without changing the normal mail actions. RFC 5435 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8580.

today: RFC 5435 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2009. The unit metadata says RFC 8580 updates it.

sections.title: The enotify Extension
sections.content:
Sieve is a language for rules that process incoming email. This RFC adds the notify action so a rule can request a notification while processing a message.

The RFC does not define every way to deliver a notification. It requires support for the mailto method, while other methods depend on the server and its configuration. A script requests the extension with the capability name enotify.
sections.plainLanguage: A Sieve script can ask for a notice when it processes a message. The script can use email for this, and a server may also support other delivery methods.

sections.title: The notify Action and Its Method
sections.content:
The action takes optional tags for the sender, importance, method-specific options, and message text, followed by a required method URI. The method determines how the notification is formatted; the text supplied with :message SHOULD be included.

The URI names a notification method, such as mailto, tel, or XMPP. An unsupported method, invalid URI syntax, or unsupported URI extension causes a run-time error. The action does not cancel Sieve's implicit keep, and a script may run more than one notify action.
sections.plainLanguage: The action names a delivery method and can include text, a sender, and an importance level. If the server cannot use the named method, the script encounters an error while it runs.

sections.title: Importance, Options and Message Text
sections.content:
The :importance tag accepts 1 for high, 2 for normal, or 3 for low importance. If the tag is absent, the method SHOULD treat the value as 2. A method without importance support MUST ignore the tag.

The :from tag identifies the notification author, with syntax defined by the method. The :options tag passes method-specific values; this RFC defines none. The :message tag supplies text, which may be shortened for technical or aesthetic reasons. If omitted, a default message is used; the RFC recommends including the message's From and Subject values.
sections.plainLanguage: Importance is a small scale: one is high, two is normal, and three is low. The method may use this setting, but it must ignore it if it has no way to represent importance.

sections.title: Checking Methods Before Use
sections.content:
The valid_notify_method test checks whether every listed URI is supported and valid. Its checks MUST match the checks made when the URI is used by notify, so a script can test a method before requesting it.

The notify_method_capability test asks a method for a named capability and compares its answer with supplied values. This RFC defines online, whose possible answers are yes, no, and maybe. Even yes does not guarantee delivery. When both variables and enotify are enabled, :encodeurl percent-encodes characters that are not URI-unreserved.
sections.plainLanguage: A script can check whether a method is usable before asking it to send a notice. It can also ask whether the recipient seems available, but that answer cannot guarantee delivery.

sections.title: Security and Abuse Controls
sections.content:
A notification may travel over a path that does not protect its contents. Incorrect parameters can send information to an unintended recipient, and some methods may allow forged notifications or altered timestamps.

Methods MUST provide ways to prevent notification loops, administrators MUST be able to limit how many notify actions a script performs, and implementations MUST provide logging. Implementations SHOULD avoid allowing message-derived values to choose a notification destination, because this can create an open relay. Stored scripts also need protection from unauthorized changes and access.
sections.plainLanguage: A notification can expose information or be sent to the wrong destination. Limits, logging, careful destination checks, and protection of stored scripts reduce these risks.

sections.title: Registered Extension and Capabilities
sections.content:
IANA registered the Sieve capability enotify and created registries for notification mechanisms and notification-capability parameters. The mechanism registry had no initial entries.

Vendor-controlled names begin with vnd. and follow the registration format specified by the RFC. The first registered notification capability is online, with the values yes, no, and maybe.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC establishes official names for notification methods and capabilities. Scripts and servers can use these shared names to describe what they support.
